scenes.sub: One name, several functions. The compiler picks by argument types.
scenes.say: Function overloading. One name, several functions, and the compiler picks the right one for you.

scenes.head: Same name, different parameters
scenes.say: Overloading means several functions share one name, but differ in their parameter types or count. Call print with forty two, and the compiler sees an int, so it picks the int version. With three point one four, it picks double. With a string, it picks the string version. This choice happens entirely at compile time. That's why overloading is called compile time polymorphism.

scenes.head: Under the hood: name mangling
scenes.say: How can three functions share a name? Under the hood, the compiler mangles each name, encoding it with its parameter types. So the linker sees three completely different symbols. i for int, d for double. This is also why C code can't call them directly without extern C.

scenes.head: Two traps
scenes.say: Two traps. Return type alone doesn't count. These two parse functions look identical to a caller, so it's an error. And calls can be ambiguous. Five is an int, and converting it to long or to double are equally good, so the compiler gives up.
